title: Functional Transcranial Doppler Ultrasound for Monitoring Cerebral Blood Flow
protocol: Set the power at a reasonably high value during the initial search for the MCA signal.
Reduce the power as much as possible while maintaining a good signal after locating the MCA.
Keep the sample volume to 8–12 mm during the initial search for the MCA signal.
Increase the gate size if the signal is difficult to find, noting that this may incorporate signals from nearby arteries into the MCA signal.
Set the gain at a medium level to keep background noise minimal but present.
Set the high-pass filter cutoff to 50–150 Hz.
Set the depth to 50 mm for adult subjects.
Locate the temporal window just in front of the ear for infants and small children.
Identify the temporal window via any subwindow for teenagers and young adults.
Determine the best signal from the posterior subwindow for teenagers and young adults.
Find the temporal window just in front of the ear for adults aged 30 years or older.
Apply enough ultrasound gel to cover the surface of the transducer.
Place the transducer on the temporal window.
Search for the MCA signal, which will generally be located slightly anterior and rostral from the location of the initial transducer scalp placement.
Adjust the angle of the transducer while keeping it in the same location relative to the scalp from rostral to caudal and posterior to anterior.
Check the color M-mode display for flow in the MCA at different depths indicated by red coloring.
Increment or decrement the signal depth in 5 mm steps.
Search for the flow signal as described in step 1.4.2.
Increase or decrease the depth until the flow signal is visible in the Doppler spectrum.
Move the transducer to a nearby position on the scalp, which is slightly more anterior.
Repeat steps 1.4.1–1.4.3.
Note the depth and maximum velocity when an optimal MCA signal is obtained.
Place a mark on the scalp with a washable makeup pen where the optimal signal was found.
Increase the depth until the signal from the bifurcation of the ICA into the MCA and ACA is noted.
Search for the optimum bifurcation spectral signal using the procedure described in step 1.4.2.
Note the depth of the bifurcation when an optimal signal is obtained.
Repeat sections 1.1–1.4 and steps 1.5.1–1.5.3 on the other side of the head for bilateral monitoring.
Adjust the fixation device to fit the subject’s approximate head size by visual inspection.
Alert the subject before placing the headset on their head.
Place the headset on the subject’s head.
Adjust the fixation device’s fit and ask the subject if the device is too tight.
Loosen the mechanism of the fixation device.
Alert the subject before applying gel to the transducers.
Apply ultrasound gel to cover the face of the transducer.
Adjust the fixation device so that the transducer is located over the mark made in step 1.4.6.
Search for the optimal MCA spectral signal using steps 1.4.1–1.4.3.
Strive for the highest-velocity spectral signal possible.
Tighten the mechanism of the fixation device to lock the transducer in place when the optimal signal is found.
Decrease the power as much as possible while maintaining accurate tracing of maximal velocity.
For bilateral monitoring, repeat steps on the other side.
Begin recording on the TCD software.
Breathe normally for 3 min to achieve a good baseline recording and allow CBFV to stabilize.
Count down slowly from three.
Ask the subject to begin breath-holding following a normal inspiration.
Place a marker in the TCD recording to signify the start of breath-holding.
Have the subject hold their breath for 30 s, or until they are no longer comfortable holding their breath.
Place a marker in the TCD recording to signify the end of breath-holding when the subject inhales.
Continue monitoring CBFV using TCD and recording for at least 30 s following the end of breath-holding.
